chapters.title: Chapter 1: Normal Glucose Homeostasis and Endocrine Pancreatic Physiology
chapters.description: Covers the integrated physiology that maintains blood glucose within a narrow range, focusing on pancreatic islet structure and function, insulin and counterregulatory hormones, and the cellular mechanisms of insulin secretion.
subtopics: Anatomy of pancreatic islets and cell types (β, α, δ, PP, ε cells)
Insulin synthesis, storage and regulated exocytosis
Glucose sensing in β-cells (GLUT transporters, glucokinase)
Stimulus–secretion coupling: ATP/ADP ratio, KATP channels, membrane depolarization, calcium influx
Counterregulatory hormones: glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol, growth hormone
Basal vs postprandial insulin secretion dynamics
Role of incretins (GLP-1, GIP) in augmenting insulin secretion

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Molecular Biology and Function of HNF1A (Hepatocyte Nuclear Factor‑1α)
chapters.description: Describes the HNF1A gene and protein structure, expression pattern, transcriptional targets, and the physiological consequences of HNF1A activity in pancreas, liver and kidney.
subtopics: HNF1A gene structure, exons and protein domains (DNA‑binding, dimerization, transactivation)
Tissue expression: pancreatic β‑cells, hepatocytes, renal tubular cells
Key transcriptional targets: insulin, GLUT2, SGLT2, metabolic enzymes (e.g., pyruvate kinase)
Role in β‑cell development, differentiation and maintenance of function
Mechanisms by which HNF1A dysfunction impairs glucose homeostasis
Genotype–phenotype correlations and domain‑specific effects

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Pathophysiology of Monogenic Diabetes (MODY) Syndromes
chapters.description: Introduces maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) as a group of monogenic, autosomal dominant diabetes disorders, their pathophysiologic mechanisms and natural history.
subtopics: Definition and distinguishing features of MODY versus type 1 and type 2 diabetes
Common MODY genes (HNF1A, GCK, HNF4A, HNF1B, others) and their mechanisms
Inheritance patterns, penetrance and variable expressivity
Typical age of onset, progression of β‑cell dysfunction and metabolic phenotype
Clinical implications of different MODY subtypes for treatment and prognosis
Overlap with polygenic type 2 diabetes and modifiers of phenotype

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Clinical Presentation and Differential Diagnosis of Early‑Onset Diabetes
chapters.description: Framework for evaluating hyperglycaemia in children, adolescents and young adults, emphasizing distinguishing features between type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes and monogenic forms.
subtopics: Typical clinical features of type 1 vs type 2 diabetes in young patients
Red flags suggesting monogenic diabetes (family history, non‑obese phenotype, atypical course)
Role of BMI, acanthosis nigricans and features of insulin resistance
Use and limitations of clinical scoring systems (MODY probability calculators)
When to suspect other forms (secondary diabetes, syndromic causes)

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Laboratory Evaluation of Hyperglycaemia — Biochemical Tests and Interpretation
chapters.description: Principles and interpretation of common glycaemic tests used to diagnose and monitor diabetes and to help subtype early‑onset diabetes.
subtopics: Fasting plasma glucose, random glucose and diagnostic thresholds
Glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c): physiology, diagnostic criteria, limitations
Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT): indications and interpretation
Urine glucose and glycosuria: renal threshold physiology
Lipid panel abnormalities commonly associated with diabetes
Use of home blood glucose monitoring and continuous glucose monitoring (CGM)

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Assessment of Endogenous Insulin Secretion: C‑peptide and Stimulation Tests
chapters.description: Describes measurement of C‑peptide to assess endogenous insulin production and the utility of stimulation tests in clinical decision making.
subtopics: Biology of proinsulin, insulin and C‑peptide; kinetics and assay characteristics
Fasting vs stimulated C‑peptide measurements (mixed‑meal, glucagon stimulation)
Interpretation of absolute values and cutoffs for preserved β‑cell function
Clinical scenarios where C‑peptide is informative (distinguishing type 1 vs non‑type 1)
Limitations and confounders (renal function, exogenous insulin)

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Autoimmune Markers in Diabetes — GADA, IA‑2, ZnT8 and Others
chapters.description: Covers the role and interpretation of diabetes autoantibodies in identifying type 1 autoimmune diabetes and their limitations in excluding other diagnoses.
subtopics: Pathophysiology of autoimmune β‑cell destruction
Common diabetes autoantibodies: GAD65 (GADA), IA‑2, insulin autoantibodies (IAA), ZnT8
Sensitivity, specificity and timing of autoantibody testing
Prevalence of autoantibodies in various clinical contexts (new‑onset, latent autoimmune diabetes)
Situations with autoantibody positivity in non‑type 1 diabetes and false negatives

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Molecular Genetic Testing Methods and Interpretation for Monogenic Diabetes
chapters.description: Details the laboratory methods used to detect monogenic diabetes variants, bioinformatic pipelines, and principles for clinical interpretation and reporting.
subtopics: Genetic testing modalities: Sanger sequencing, targeted panels, next‑generation sequencing (NGS), exome/genome sequencing
Coverage, sensitivity, limitations and variant types detected (missense, nonsense, indels, splice site, CNVs)
Laboratory workflows: sample preparation, alignment, variant calling and quality control
Variant databases (ClinVar, gnomAD) and in silico prediction tools
Segregation analysis and family testing

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Variant Classification and the ACMG/AMP Guidelines
chapters.description: Explains the framework used to classify genetic variants (pathogenic, likely pathogenic, VUS, likely benign, benign) and the evidence categories applied clinically.
subtopics: Overview of ACMG/AMP criteria and evidence weightings (population data, computational, functional, segregation, de novo, allelic, phenotype)
Examples of evidence types that support pathogenic vs benign classification
Approach to variants of uncertain significance (VUS) and reclassification considerations
Clinical reporting standards and implications for patient management
Limitations of in silico predictors and population database biases

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Genetic Epidemiology and Inheritance Counseling for MODY
chapters.description: Provides knowledge about the frequency, penetrance and familial transmission of monogenic diabetes and principles of genetic counselling for affected families.
subtopics: Prevalence estimates of MODY in different populations and ascertainment biases
Autosomal dominant inheritance, variable penetrance and age‑dependent expressivity
Recurrence risks, cascade screening strategies and testing of relatives
Ethical, legal and psychosocial issues in genetic testing
Implications for reproductive counselling and prenatal testing

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Pharmacology of Diabetes Therapies Relevant to MODY
chapters.description: Mechanisms of action, clinical uses and adverse effect profiles of major glucose‑lowering agents, with emphasis on therapies commonly used for HNF1A‑related diabetes.
subtopics: Sulfonylureas and meglitinides: KATP channel agonism, dosage considerations and hypoglycaemia risk
Metformin: mechanism (hepatic glucose output reduction), indications and contraindications
GLP‑1 receptor agonists: incretin agonism, effects on insulin secretion, weight and cardiovascular outcomes
DPP‑4 inhibitors: mechanism and comparative efficacy
Insulin therapy: basal and bolus regimens, indications for initiation and discontinuation
SGLT2 inhibitors: renal glucose reabsorption blockade, benefits and risks (DKA, genitourinary infections, volume depletion)

chapters.title: Chapter 12: Rationale for Therapy Selection in Monogenic Diabetes (Precision Treatment Principles)
chapters.description: Discusses how specific genetic etiologies of diabetes inform individualized therapy choices and monitoring strategies.
subtopics: Evidence linking genotype to drug responsiveness (e.g., sulfonylurea sensitivity in HNF1A‑MODY)
When to prefer oral agents vs insulin in different MODY subtypes
Monitoring strategies after therapy change and risk mitigation (hypoglycaemia, DKA)
Role of non‑glycaemic benefits (weight, cardiovascular risk) in agent selection
Clinical trial evidence and guideline recommendations for monogenic diabetes

chapters.title: Chapter 13: Renal Physiology of Glucose Handling and Glycosuria
chapters.description: Covers the mechanisms of renal glucose filtration and reabsorption, transporters involved (SGLT2, SGLT1, GLUTs) and causes of low renal threshold for glucose.
subtopics: Glomerular filtration of glucose and tubular reabsorption dynamics
Sodium–glucose cotransporters (SGLT2 in proximal tubule S1, SGLT1 in S3): expression and regulation
Genetic and acquired causes of glycosuria (familial renal glucosuria, transporter downregulation)
Clinical implications of decreased renal glucose threshold (dehydration, electrolyte loss)
Impact of SGLT2 inhibitors and interplay with underlying transporter expression

chapters.title: Chapter 14: Autonomic Neuropathy and Small Fibre Dysfunction Testing
chapters.description: Introduction to diabetic autonomic neuropathy, methods to assess small fibre function including sweat function testing, and interpretation in clinical practice.
subtopics: Pathophysiology of diabetic autonomic and small fibre neuropathy
Clinical manifestations (cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, sudomotor)
Testing modalities: QSART, thermoregulatory sweat testing, Sudoscan/electrochemical skin conductance
Interpretation of results and limitations of non‑invasive autonomic tests
Implications for monitoring and management

chapters.title: Chapter 15: Screening and Management of Microvascular and Macrovascular Complications in Diabetes
chapters.description: Outlines standard approaches to screen for and prevent diabetes complications, including nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy and cardiovascular disease.
subtopics: Screening intervals and tests: urine albumin/creatinine ratio, retinal examination, foot sensory testing
Risk factors for complication development and intensification based on glycaemic exposure
Primary prevention strategies: glycaemic targets, blood pressure and lipid management
Acute complications (DKA, hyperosmolar state) and risk factors
Long‑term surveillance and multidisciplinary care

chapters.title: Chapter 16: Diagnostic Algorithms and Clinical Tools for Suspecting MODY
chapters.description: Reviews clinical algorithms and scoring systems used to identify candidates for genetic testing for MODY and discusses limitations and population considerations.
subtopics: Components of clinical algorithms (age of onset, family history, autoantibody status, C‑peptide)
Use and interpretation of MODY probability calculators (strengths and limitations)
Cost‑effectiveness and indications for targeted vs broad genetic testing
Population differences and pitfalls in applying tools developed in one ethnic group to others
Practical workflow from clinical suspicion to genetic confirmation

chapters.title: Chapter 17: Bioinformatics and Functional Prediction of Missense Variants
chapters.description: Describes computational approaches to predict the functional impact of amino acid substitutions and the interpretation of such predictions in a clinical context.
subtopics: Principles of in silico predictors (conservation, structural modeling, machine learning)
Common tools and scores (PolyPhen, SIFT, CADD, REVEL, newer models like AlphaMissense-type predictors)
Strengths and limitations of computational evidence for pathogenicity
Integration of computational data with other evidence (functional assays, segregation, population frequency)
Guidelines for the responsible use of predictive scores in reporting

chapters.title: Chapter 18: Principles of Next‑Generation Sequencing for Clinical Diagnostics
chapters.description: Technical overview of NGS technology as applied to clinical genetic testing, focusing on design choices, quality metrics and interpretative caveats.
subtopics: Sequencing chemistry, read lengths, and platforms used in clinical labs
Panel design vs exome vs genome sequencing: tradeoffs and typical use cases
Depth of coverage, target uniformity and limits of detection
Bioinformatic QC metrics, variant calling and annotation pipelines
Clinical accreditation, validation, reporting standards and variant reanalysis policies

chapters.title: Chapter 19: Principles of Precision Medicine and Translational Genomic Reporting
chapters.description: Introduces the concept of precision medicine applied to monogenic diseases, including how genetic information informs therapy, surveillance and family management.
subtopics: Definition and goals of precision medicine in endocrine disorders
Translating genotype to phenotype: actionable findings and therapeutic implications
Designing individualized monitoring and prevention plans based on genetic diagnosis
Reporting actionable results and communicating uncertainty to patients
Health systems considerations: access to testing, cost, and equitable implementation
